Quality worth making room for

Prefer Newsroom on Google

NZ First’s newest candidate says the party offers voters a chance to curtail the influence of academics and return to the fundamentals of Western civilisation.

Elliot Ikilei spent time in other parties before joining NZ First and has made headlines for his controversial social commentary – a background shared by several of the party’s recent additions.

But Ikilei argues his background as a youth advocate and connections with the Pacific community offer a more genuine option for voters who are sick of the status quo, as NZ First enjoys some of the highest polling data it’s seen in a generation.

Before joining the party, Ikilei had a stint as the leader of the New Conservatives and is the head spokesperson for Hobson’s Pledge, which advocates against “race-based” legislation.

He’s no stranger to politics, and just last year had a back-and-forth with Education Minister Erica Stanford over Treaty of Waitangi obligations regarding school boards. Ikilei said she was placing a “radical” clause in the legislation; Stanford said Hobson’s Pledge was “spouting complete and utter garbage”.

Ikilei is the second Hobson’s Pledge spokesperson to run for NZ First. Cabinet minister Casey Costello ran in 2023, and was ranked third overall on the party list (this year’s list hasn’t been released, and Ikilei doesn’t know where he will be placed).

Speaking to Newsroom, Ikilei says his background and ideologies reflect the viewpoints of more New Zealanders than Parliament might think: “We see common sense becoming less common sense.”

He doesn’t think either major party – Labour or National – has done enough to represent the people. Ikilei, with a Tongan, Niuean, Māori and English background, says he’s sick and tired of people treating his race as “some inferior citizen”.

“One thing our opponents cannot do is somehow try to proclaim us to be racist,” Ikilei says, arguing NZ First offers “authentic, organic diversity”.

“There’s no quota system nonsense going on, as I suspect there is in other parties.”

Labour has historically seen success with Pacific voters, but Ikilei thinks he has more on-the-ground experience where it matters, while established parties are unable to resonate with many of the issues these voters really care about.

Some of these issues, like being “proud to put New Zealand’s needs first”, are boilerplate. Others, like defining a woman, are more fringe.

Ikilei says fringe views aren’t limited to fringe spaces, and the modern status quo represented by establishment parties “has become somewhat fringe itself”.

Around the world, from the United States to Australia – and “obviously France and Canada” – academics have gained more incursion into the policy space. These academics, “unfortunately disconnected from our normal day to day life”, don’t represent the interests of the working class, says Ikilei.

He says their influence has manifested as a slew of leftist policies, paving the way for the normalisation of sexual “depravities”, entrenched globalism and climate “alarmism”.

“The anger that I, as a conservative, have is that we believe children should be left alone. We do not want our children indoctrinated with transgender ideology, with climate change alarmism, with racial bigotry.

“We do not want that, and we see the children being indoctrinated with such leftist ideologies as that, and it’s unacceptable.”

He says the best thing to do is leave children alone. “Let us oldies have to fight these battles – it’s unfair to load them up with the destiny of a nation.”

Ikilei sees a global reaction to “leftist policies” championed overseas: by Reform in the United Kingdom, One Nation in Australia, and Donald Trump in the United States. “And in New Zealand, you’ve got NZ First.”

Academics are still important, he says, but need to be balanced out by voices from all constituencies – including those who understand the “objective moral boundaries” needed to uphold the foundations of Western civilisation: Greek democracy and Judeo-Christian principles.

Ikilei thinks he brings a middle ground to the table. He has front line experience working in youth support – ranging from “the more horrific stuff” to team-bonding exercises – and believes he understands people on a deeper level than most entrenched politicians. This is compounded with his experience as the spokesperson for Hobson’s Pledge and political involvement.

He can also bring an academic perspective, “not that I’m an academic”.

“I’ve been able to do enough study to be able to bring academic and real-world principles together to be mixed in what I would regard as a more appropriate understanding of life.”

University of Otago political scholar David Jenkins keeps an eye on populist movements worldwide and says many of Ikilei’s points are classic populist strategies, particularly the “do your own research” approach.

But Jenkins says Ikilei offers something voters could be hungry for: authenticity, regardless of ideology.

For members of establishment parties, the track is pretty cut and dry: do well at school, go to a top university and study politics or economics, get high marks, then join the youth wing of your party. “That is essentially their political experience,” he says.

For anyone else, if you can’t take that route, an established party is probably either out of reach or unfamiliar, making it very difficult for voters to relate to their representatives.

“In terms of the nitty-gritty, ideologically committed candidates who we’re supposed to elect on the basis of their ideas and their principles – especially when I look at the UK – it’s like, where are they?”

Jenkins says Ikilei is doing something very few entrenched politicians have done, offering a background genuinely spent “in the trenches”.

This isn’t as available in the major parties with their established pipelines, but it is more and more common in smaller parties worldwide, on both sides of the aisle. For lack of a better word, these are “plebeian candidates, people that don’t really belong to a political class”.

Candidates with fringe views like Ikilei’s don’t find a home in major parties, Jenkins says, because those parties have “evolved to marginalise their fringes to contain the kind of threat that they pose, while at the same time bringing them in as activists and people that will knock on doors”.

The result is a chance for fringe parties to take on more colourful candidates, in the hopes that their ideological platform will appeal to voters more than the more technical platforms of established parties.

Ikilei thinks NZ First is doing “an extremely brave thing” by taking such an approach into this election. With the party polling higher than it has in decades, it’s poised to take on a more influential role after the November election.

22 Comments

“…NZ First’s newest candidate wants to protect youth, resist academic influence…”
How will resisting academic influence help to educate our young in the democratic world of real life? And how did a putative interview with Ikilei morph into an interview with Jenkins? Is he a Ikilei supporter, promoter or just a bystander? Seriously, do we really want another ‘tough guy’, standing for a seat in Parliament, to align us with …”Reform in the United Kingdom, One Nation in Australia, and Donald Trump in the United States.” ?? really
 “And in New Zealand, you’ve got NZ First.”…but not for long, I hope. The general ‘fascist’ tone from politics lately has given many voters a sense of unease.
Remember that Government ‘by the people’ should be for ALL the people…Including those with differing views hammered… out into a workable way of living together. Those of us old enough to remember and understand history know that fascism doesn’t work. That’s why we chose democracy – for the people. It’s a protracted way of governing… but it works!

Can’t understand why anyone is surprised when Shane Jones has echoed Trump in wearing a “Make New Zealand Great Again” hat and used the Trumpian term “drill baby drill” for oil and gas.

The entire party relies on conspiracy theorists, ignorance and bigotry.

It is certainly alarming to see NZ First leaning so far to the conservative Christian right. Just as, thank goodness, a number of other countries are seeing the light and kicking them out.

Every current in politics has its genesis in its opposite.

The far left are as responsible for NZ First’s rightward shift as any model purportedly copied from overseas.

NZ First’s latest pearl-clutchingly right-wing flirtations wouldn’t be nearly so appealing if it wasn’t for the far-left lunacy exhibited by Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Pantomime (not to mention much of the media).

Blaming an abstract ‘far-left’ is an embarrassing rewriting of basic history. NZ First spent three full years in a governing coalition with Labour and the Greens from 2017 to 2020, proudly branding themselves as a centrist handbrake. They didn’t shift to imported culture wars because of an organic ‘genesis’—they did it as a cynical, transactional branding exercise after voters in Aotearoa dumped them entirely in 2020. Regurgitating talkback-radio buzzwords to defend a trumped-up platform that offers zero solutions is the ultimate armchair comfort. It’s easy to play the profound political philosopher and make excuses for actors exploiting real voter pain when you are risking absolutely nothing, cowering from behind a keyboard.

NZ First scare me. In addition to Ikilei, they are also hoovering up ousted and disgruntled ex-mayors. They appeal to us with their simple answers to increasingly complex questions and their blame game. It resonates with people who are under constant pressure, who don’t know what to believe and who to trust, let alone what to do and where to start. I wonder if we will make the same mistake as so many other Western democracies and go through a prolonged period of cruel and chaotic government, before we eventually realise that there is absolutely no future in it that would ensure our collective well-being within ecological limits.

Appalling – but probably what I now expect from NZ First.

There’s some indoctrination going on alright, but it’s not from academics or the LGBTQ+ community. It just confirms that NZ First has become a repository for bigots and nutjobs.

No flies on this guy. It reminds me of Anthony ‘The Mooch’ Scaramucci, who campaigned with Trump. He reckoned that as soon as he stepped off the stage, he looked around and said, ‘I can’t believe they believe this shit.’ Meanwhile, this candidate walks off the stage and straight into a guaranteed, taxpayer-funded goldmine: a $175,944 base salary, a 2.5-to-1 superannuation match (up to $36,240), a $36,400 capital accommodation allowance, and $16,980 in basic expenses. The crowd gets the performance, and he gets the prize.

You can spot superficial similarities at an electoral level, but fail to mention that the most important similarities are the circumstances giving rise to this populism.

I failed nothing in my analysis—I merely focused on the subject matter—NZ First’s latest trumped-up candidate rather than the prey. However, my history includes having been headhunted by the late Marcia Read QSO to volunteer as a counsellor for what was then the Phobic Trust for over a decade. I understand community trauma and societal fracture at the absolute frontline, including inside a maximum-security psychiatric hospital. I chose to support vulnerable people for free, rather than use their pain as a stepping stone to a $175,000 political salary plus salubrious perks.

Mainstream politicians operate on policy platforms within established frameworks, but NZ First has increasingly transformed into a sanctuary for political outcasts and dissidents. A look at their current crop reveals an erratic patchwork of conflicting political histories—a volatile mix that thrives on ‘rage-baiting’. They deliberately manufacture fear and anti-establishment grievance, offering zero actual solutions, purely to cash in on the anger of the people they claim to represent. Acknowledging that vulnerable people can be manipulated by this slick showmanship isn’t insulting their intelligence; it’s recognising the power of a calculated marketing campaign.

History is littered with communities hurting from economic anxiety who were sold a false populist dream by actors chasing power. Nor is this about gatekeeping; it’s about accountability. When people sit in a comment section defending a political strategy that exploits community pain for a taxpayer prize, it is entirely fair to ask whether they speak from real-world experience on the frontlines, or from the comfort of an armchair. I spent that time 24/7 on call on the frontlines trying to mend that fracture for zero financial gain—what exactly, incidentally, if any, has been your contribution to easing these circumstances, other than making excuses for the people exploiting them?

I think the neo-liberal and conservative parties have abandoned ‘Judeo-Christian morality’ some time ago – just look at Nixon and Bush’s war, Blair’s war, Putin’s war, Netanyahu’s war, and Trump’s war – what’s judeo-christian about them? Maybe we need more buddhists, who still know what morality is.

Thank you, Desmond! All joking aside, I agree. But even Buddhists have turned feral in recent times (was it in Sri Lanka, where they turned on each other?). Let’s look inside our own individual hearts…and vote accordingly.

It is always amusing when governments come to believe their own propaganda but when our own politicians swallow US propaganda hook line and sinker, then we should begin to worry, as when Peters in early March come out to tell us that the US/Israeli war against Iran would be over in a few days.  It is all the way with the USA for NZ First, not just with foreign policy but in taking aim against “woke” policies, WHO, and the UN, and in taking on board fundamentalist Xtians like Ikekei and Alfred Ngaro who through the Israel Institute of NZ supports Israel’s genocidal activities and the biblical greater Israel..

Elliot is quite correct.  The US has Trump, Britain has Farage, Australia has Hansen and we have Peters / Jones.  A very sad situation.

Neil – from a different view of the political spectrum, how about “The US has/had Biden, Britain has Starmer, Australia has Albanese, NZ has/had Ardern/Hipkins…..a very sad situation”

Equating Albanese, Ardern, or Hipkins to Trump, Farage, and Hanson is laughable, John. There’s a massive gulf between mainstream leaders and a group of verified conspiracy theorists, convicted felons, and professional grifters. What makes it a total comedy of errors is that Elliot is auditioning for a global circus of useful idiots whose figureheads built careers on anti-immigrant rhetoric, while Jones is already busy copy-pasting the Trump playbook for local headlines. The cognitive dissonance of two men of proud Polynesian heritage rushing to align with white identity politics for cheap populism is staggering.

Thanks for this article, Fox. I appreciate Jenkins’ comment that voters may be hungry for ‘authenticity regardless of ideology’. People hope that their representatives will be like them, or at least to understand what it is like to be them. Ikilei’s experience as a social worker will appeal and he is likely to be able to communicate with people who are perceived as or feel themselves to be ‘inferior citizens’.
I’m an academic lefty. I struggle to accept others’ very different views on what we need to protect children from, what Judaeo-Christian morality comprises or Western civilisation means.  However, the people out there are not ‘bigots’ or ‘nut jobs’ because they’re different.
The aim of the major parties should be to connect with them and find out what would win their vote.  Condemning them as ‘deplorables’ is the way to let in Trumpism.

Wise words, Chris.

I’m hungry for authenticity, too, although for one that ensures our and the planet’s well-being within ecological limits, rather than yet another alternative truth.

I agree Chris.
Well put. The mainstream parties are suffering from being easily boxed and in the process losing voters and promoting the very conditions Trumpism will develop

This open acknowledgement must be the starting point for anyone deciding whether to “vote for Winston”. Ikilei sees a global reaction to “leftist policies” championed overseas: by Reform in the United Kingdom, One Nation in Australia, and Donald Trump in the United States. “And in New Zealand, you’ve got NZ First.” Trump’s war against Iran drags on, the world pays the price and the Iranians somehow, against the overwhelming might of the US military, make fun of Trump and refuse to bow to his demands. It’s difficult to understand why Kiwi voters would choose a party that aligns with the Trump regime and sets out to recreate it in our little South Pacific paradise.  But hey, right now the polls are saying “voters who are sick of the status quo” genuinely believe we’d be better off with an 81 year-old right-wing populist leader.

Absolutely awfulness from these populist parties. We are going backwards in terms of humanity. It’s pretty obvious that our country is not the kindly little country we thought we were. But these anti immigrant sentiments are being exploited by Winston and his ilk, and that’s extremely worrisome. We need pushback from our more progressive parties and to ask our coalition Govt as to their solutions on homelessness, jobs and social cohesion. Just listening to Helen Robinson from the Auckland City Mission on our homeless whānau. Totally scandalous.
